sections.title: Workstation Hardening
sections.content:
Hardening is the process of reducing a system's attack surface by disabling unnecessary functionality, changing insecure defaults, and applying the minimum required configuration for the system's intended function.
Change default administrator credentials: the default administrator account name â€” typically "Administrator" on Windows â€” and any default password are publicly known. Attackers attempt these credentials as a first step. Rename the built-in Administrator account to a non-obvious name. Set a strong, unique password. This applies not just to workstations but to all devices â€” routers, switches, printers, access points.
Disable the guest account: the Windows guest account provides access to the system without a password. It is disabled by default in modern Windows but should be explicitly verified. An enabled guest account provides a foothold for local access without any credential requirement.
Disable AutoRun: AutoRun is the feature that automatically executes programs when removable media â€” USB drives, CDs, DVDs â€” is inserted. Malware spread via AutoRun infected millions of systems before the feature was disabled by default in Windows 7. AutoRun is disabled by default in modern Windows but should be verified through Group Policy â€” particularly in enterprise environments where some systems may have older configurations.
Disable unused services: every service running on a system represents a potential attack vector â€” an exploitable code path, a network listener that could be targeted. Identify which services the system requires for its function and disable everything else. Remote Desktop Protocol â€” RDP â€” should be disabled on systems where remote administration is not needed. Telnet should be disabled on all systems â€” it transmits credentials in cleartext. The Print Spooler service has been the target of multiple critical vulnerabilities and should be disabled on servers that do not print. Document what is disabled and why.
BIOS and UEFI passwords: the supervisor password â€” also called administrator password â€” controls access to BIOS/UEFI settings and has the highest privilege level. A user with supervisor password access can change the boot order, disable Secure Boot, and alter any system configuration. The user password is required to boot the computer but provides limited access to BIOS settings. Both passwords prevent unauthorized boot order changes â€” including booting from a USB drive or live CD, which could be used to bypass OS-level access controls entirely.
Screensaver lock and session timeout: a workstation left unattended at a logged-in session is an open door. Configure the screensaver to require a password after activation, and set the screensaver timeout to five to fifteen minutes. Enforce this through Group Policy in domain environments. Users should also be trained to manually lock their workstation â€” Windows+L â€” when stepping away from the desk, even briefly.
Log off when not in use: more secure than locking. Logging off terminates the session, closes all running applications, and releases any network connections. Required in high-security environments where other users share the physical space.
Account management controls: least privilege â€” users should operate as standard users, not administrators, for daily work. Administrator accounts should be used only for specific administrative tasks. Restrict login times â€” Active Directory allows configuration of hours during which an account is permitted to authenticate. Useful for limiting off-hours access by employees whose job function does not require it.
Failed login attempt lockout: configure accounts to lock after a defined number of failed authentication attempts â€” typically three to five. This prevents brute-force attacks against the password. Locked accounts require administrator intervention to unlock, which creates an audit trail. Too aggressive a lockout threshold â€” one or two attempts â€” can create denial-of-service conditions through accidental lockouts.
Account expiration dates: Active Directory allows setting an expiration date on a user account, after which it is automatically disabled. Essential for contractor and temporary staff accounts. Without expiration dates, accounts for departed personnel remain active until someone manually disables them â€” which may never happen.
Secure and protect critical hardware: physical security is the foundation of workstation security. Cable locks secure laptops to desks. Server rooms should be locked. Physical access to a machine bypasses most software security controls. A person with physical access and a bootable USB drive can access the contents of an unencrypted drive.
Data-at-rest encryption: BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS, LUKS on Linux. Encrypts the drive so that physical theft of the machine does not result in data exposure. The drive is unreadable without the encryption key and authentication.
---
exam_tips: Change default credentials is ALWAYS the first hardening step. Disable AutoRun prevents malware from self-executing from USB drives. Guest account has no password â€” disable it. BIOS supervisor password > user password in privilege level.

sections.title: Password Policies
sections.content:
A password policy defines the requirements that all passwords in the environment must meet.
Length: minimum eight characters for basic compliance. Twelve or more characters is the current recommendation. Password length is the strongest determinant of crack resistance â€” each additional character exponentially increases the search space.
Complexity: requiring uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters increases entropy. However, modern guidance from NIST deprioritizes mandatory complexity requirements in favor of length and uniqueness, because complexity requirements often lead to predictable patterns â€” "Password1!" meets most complexity requirements while being extremely weak.
Uniqueness: each account should have a unique password. Password reuse across systems means a credential breach at one site enables access to all others where that password is reused. Password managers are the practical solution â€” they generate and store unique, random passwords for each account.
Expiration: traditional policy forces password changes every sixty to ninety days. The modern NIST guidance recommends against mandatory rotation unless a credential compromise is known â€” because forced rotation often results in predictable passwords like "Spring2024!" with minor variations.
No personal information: passwords should not contain the user's name, username, birthdate, or other easily guessed personal data.
Account password history: prevents reuse of recent passwords when a password change is required.
---
exam_tips: Swipe = zero security. Pattern = smudge attack vulnerability (oily screen residue reveals pattern). Facial recognition security depends on implementation â€” 3D infrared (Face ID) is much more secure than 2D camera. Six-digit minimum PIN for business use.

sections.title: Mobile Device Security
sections.content:
Screen lock methods â€” five types appear on the A+ exam.
Facial recognition: iOS Face ID uses a three-dimensional infrared map of the face â€” highly accurate and resistant to photo spoofing. Older 2D facial recognition systems on Android can be defeated by a photograph of the owner's face. Fast and convenient for daily use.
Fingerprint: Touch ID on iOS, integrated sensors on Android. Fast biometric authentication. More secure than a PIN. Requires a backup authentication method â€” PIN or passcode â€” for situations where the biometric sensor fails.
PIN: four to six digit numeric code. Six digits minimum is recommended. A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possible combinations â€” limited resistance to targeted guessing. Vulnerable to shoulder surfing. Simple and fast.
Pattern: available on Android. The user draws a path across a grid of dots to unlock. Easy to remember. Vulnerable to smudge attacks â€” the pattern is visible as oily residue on the screen. Not recommended for high-security environments.
Swipe: a simple swipe gesture to dismiss the lock screen. Provides no security whatsoever â€” only prevents accidental input. Never acceptable for business or corporate use.
Device encryption: full device encryption is enabled by default on iOS when a passcode is set. On Android, encryption is typically enabled by default on modern devices but varies. Encrypts the internal storage so the data is unreadable without authentication â€” protects against physical theft and forensic data extraction.
Failed login attempt restrictions: configure the device to lock or wipe after a defined number of failed unlock attempts. iOS can be configured to erase after ten failed attempts. Android increases the delay between attempts. Enforced through MDM configuration profiles.
Operating system and application updates: mobile OS updates contain security patches. Enable automatic updates on both iOS and Android. Application updates close vulnerabilities in installed apps. Install apps only from official stores â€” Apple App Store and Google Play Store â€” and review requested permissions before installation.
Endpoint security: antivirus and anti-malware are less common on iOS due to the sandboxed application model, but available for Android. Content filtering blocks access to malicious or inappropriate websites. Deployed through MDM profiles.
Locator applications: Find My on iOS and Find My Device on Android use GPS to locate a lost or stolen device. Can display a custom message on the locked screen, play an audible sound, remotely lock the device, and trigger a remote wipe. These features must be enabled before the device is lost â€” they cannot be activated after the fact on a device that was never enrolled.
Remote wipe: erases all data on the device. Triggered through Find My, MDM, or Exchange ActiveSync. The device must be online to receive the command â€” if the device is offline, the command queues and executes when the device next connects. Cannot be undone. Should always be paired with remote backup to enable restoration on a replacement device.
Remote backup: iCloud for iOS, Google Drive for Android. Automatically backs up device data â€” photos, contacts, app data, settings. After a remote wipe, backup data can be restored to a replacement device. Verify that backups are completing successfully and are current.
---
exam_tips: Remote wipe command queues if the device is offline â€” executes when device next connects to internet. Locator apps (Find My, Find My Device) must be enabled BEFORE the device is lost. Remote backup enables restoration after a wipe.

sections.title: Mdm And Byod
sections.content:
Mobile Device Management â€” MDM: enterprise platform for centrally managing mobile device fleets. IT administrators use MDM to deploy configuration profiles, enforce security policies, push application installations, track device inventory, monitor compliance status, and execute remote wipes. MDM examples include Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE, and Jamf Pro.
Configuration profiles: pre-built policy packages pushed to devices remotely. Can enforce password requirements, screen lock timeout, encryption settings, VPN configurations, Wi-Fi network profiles, email account setup, and usage restrictions. Users cannot modify settings enforced by a profile â€” the profile overrides local settings.
BYOD â€” Bring Your Own Device: employees use personal devices for work tasks. Introduces security challenges. The device is not fully managed â€” the employee has personal data on the device alongside corporate data. Privacy concerns limit how aggressively MDM can monitor and control personal devices. Containerization â€” isolating corporate apps and data in a separate encrypted container â€” is the primary mitigation. The container can be remotely wiped without affecting personal data.
Corporate-owned devices: the organization owns and controls the device entirely. Full MDM enforcement with no privacy limitations. Can be completely wiped without concern for personal data. Preferred for high-security roles where data exposure would be severe.
Profile security requirements: MDM can enforce minimum security requirements before a device is permitted to connect to corporate resources. A device without a screen lock, without current patches, or with a jailbroken OS can be blocked from accessing email and internal applications until it meets compliance requirements.
---
exam_tips: BYOD = personal device with work data = privacy vs security tension. Containerization isolates corporate data in an encrypted container that can be wiped without touching personal data. Corporate-owned = full MDM control, no privacy limitations.

BitLocker = Windows (Pro+). FileVault = macOS. LUKS = Linux. Each is full disk encryption. iOS encrypts automatically when a passcode is set. Know which tool belongs to which OS â€” the exam will mix them.

concept_cards.summary: Workstation hardening is the process of reducing the attack surface of a system by applying a defined set of security controls. Change default credentials: default administrator account names and passwords are publicly documented for every OS and device.

concept_cards.hook: One of the five mobile screen lock methods provides zero security. If you do not know which one it is, the exam will catch you.

concept_cards.hook: A sales rep leaves a company phone in an airport. By the time IT finds out, the data is already at risk. Remote wipe exists for exactly this scenario â€” but only if it was configured before the device was lost.

practice_questions.q: What is the FIRST security action to take when setting up a new workstation?
options: Change all default passwords and update the OS with all patches

practice_questions.q: What type of software should be kept updated to ensure it can detect the latest malware?
options: Antivirus and anti-malware software (definitions and engine)

practice_questions.q: What is the purpose of a host-based firewall such as Windows Firewall?
options: Filter incoming and outgoing traffic on the individual computer

practice_questions.q: What security principle means "never trust, always verify" â€” requiring authentication and authorization for every access request regardless of location?
A technician is setting up a standard user account for a new employee. Why is a standard account preferred over an administrator account for daily use?
options: Limits the damage malware can do if the account is compromised

practice_questions.q: What should be done with user accounts when an employee leaves the organization?
options: Leave them active for IT use
Disable or delete the account immediately
Change the password and share it with the team

practice_questions.q: What is the best practice for handling autorun when inserting USB drives?
options: Only allow autorun for trusted brands
Disable autorun/autoplay to prevent automatic execution of potentially malicious code

practice_questions.q: A company policy requires workstations to automatically lock after inactivity and require re-authentication. Which Windows feature enforces this?
practice_questions.explanation: The screen saver timeout combined with "On resume, display logon screen" (enforced via Group Policy) is the standard Windows mechanism for automatic workstation locking after inactivity.

practice_questions.q: A technician is hardening a new Windows workstation. Which action BEST demonstrates applying the principle of least privilege?
options: Creating a separate administrator account for administrative tasks and using a standard account for daily use
Granting the standard user account local administrator rights to simplify software installs
Disabling Windows Defender to allow all applications to run without restrictions
Configuring the firewall to allow all outbound traffic by default
practice_questions.explanation: Using a standard account for daily tasks and a separate administrator account only when needed limits the damage any malware or mistake can cause, implementing least privilege at the user level.

practice_questions.q: A technician wants to prevent users from running unauthorized applications on company workstations without blocking the entire OS. Which Windows Enterprise feature allows application whitelisting?
practice_questions.explanation: AppLocker allows administrators to define rules permitting or denying specific applications, scripts, and installer files based on file path, publisher signature, or hash. It is the primary application whitelisting tool in Windows Enterprise and Education editions.

practice_questions.q: What mobile security feature wipes the device after a specified number of failed unlock attempts?
options: Failed login wipe or remote wipe after threshold

practice_questions.q: What MDM capability allows an IT admin to lock or wipe a lost corporate mobile device remotely?
What is "BYOD" and what is the primary security concern?
options: Bring Your Own Device â€” concern is mixing personal and corporate data on unmanaged devices
Buy Your Own Device â€” concern is cost
Build Your Own Device â€” concern is compatibility
Backup Your Own Data â€” concern is compliance

practice_questions.q: What type of screen lock is considered the most secure on mobile devices?
options: Strong alphanumeric passcode or biometric with backup passcode

practice_questions.q: What security feature on mobile devices verifies each app is from a trusted source before installation?
options: App signing and app store vetting (e.g., Play Protect, App Store review)

practice_questions.q: A company issues smartphones to employees and requires that all corporate data be erasable from any device reported lost or stolen. Which mobile device management capability satisfies this?
practice_questions.explanation: Remote wipe allows an administrator via MDM to send a command that erases all data on the device over the network. GPS helps locate a device but does not protect data on it.

practice_questions.q: An employee enrolls their personal smartphone in the company MDM solution for BYOD access to corporate resources. Which security concern does MDM enrollment PRIMARILY address?
options: Enforcing security policies such as screen lock, encryption, and remote wipe on the personal device
Preventing the employee from making personal calls during work hours
Blocking all personal app installations on the employee's device
Automatically upgrading device hardware to meet corporate standards
practice_questions.explanation: MDM enrollment allows IT to enforce baseline security policies on personal devices accessing corporate resources, balancing employee privacy with corporate data protection requirements.

practice_questions.q: The IT department wants to ensure that if the physical storage chip is removed from a corporate smartphone, stored data cannot be read by an attacker. Which feature provides this protection?
practice_questions.explanation: Full device encryption encrypts all data on internal storage using a key derived from the user's PIN or password. Without the decryption key, data removed on physical media is unreadable.

practice_questions.q: A mobile device requires a fingerprint scan to unlock. If the fingerprint reader fails, it falls back to a numeric PIN. Which security concept does this configuration illustrate?
options: Multi-factor authentication with a fallback method
Remote wipe triggered by failed biometric attempts
practice_questions.explanation: The fingerprint (something you are) and PIN (something you know) represent two authentication factors. The fallback ensures usability when biometrics fail, though the fallback alone is single-factor.

practice_questions.q: An organization's mobile device policy requires all apps on corporate devices to be vetted before installation. Which MDM mechanism enforces this on managed devices?
options: Corporate app catalog / MDM application whitelist
practice_questions.explanation: MDM solutions can restrict app installation to an approved corporate catalog, blocking public app stores or sideloaded packages, ensuring all applications have been reviewed for security and compliance.
